Do not turn a latent quantity or an unreported fitted quantity into a control. Use continuous_interval only when the source supports a finite interval with minimum below maximum. Record source-reported applicability or fixed context when present; otherwise use an empty applicability array.

Every formula, parameter value, control definition, readout definition, control domain, and applicability statement must carry direct inclusive source line ranges. Anchors contain line_start and line_end only. Do not generate a paraphrased support field. Use the line coordinates exactly as supplied.

L000102	\begin{abstract}
L000103	Three-dimensional spiral injection enables beam storage in ultra-compact rings with nanosecond revolution periods.
L000104	We report first storage of a $297 \,\si{keV/}c$ electron beam in a $22 \,\si{cm}$ weak-focusing ring
L000105	with a $4.7\,\si{ns}$ revolution period using a $140\,\si{ns}$ kicker pulse.
L000106	A scintillating-fiber detector observes signals $>5\sigma$ above noise for $\geq 1\,\si{\mu s}$,
L000107	and varying the weak-focusing field potential shifts the stored-beam region, consistent with Monte Carlo predictions, validating beam storage.
L000108	This proof-of-principle opens a path to ultra-compact storage rings for next-generation precision measurements.
L000109	\end{abstract}
L000110	
L000111	\maketitle
L000112	
L000113	
L000114	
L000115	
L000116	
L000117	
L000118	
L000119	{\it Introduction---}
L000120	Storage rings have played a central role in accelerator science
L000121	since their first realization as colliders in the 1960s~\cite{AdA, VEP-1, Princeton}.
L000122	Their applications now span a wide range of fields, including particle and nuclear physics,
L000123	synchrotron light sources, medical treatments, and various industrial applications.
L000124	As these applications have expanded, injection methods have undergone continuous development.
L000125	Conventional transverse injection relies on a pulsed kicker magnet
L000126	that produces a localized dipole field which steers the injected beam toward the stored orbit.
L000127	This traditional two-dimensional approach has matured over several decades
L000128	and evolved into the well-established local bump orbit technique~\cite{Lee_Textbook}.
L000129	Ongoing research has also generated next-generation concepts
L000130	such as nonlinear or multipole kicker injection~\cite{PhysRevSTAB.10.123501, PhysRevSTAB.13.020705},
L000131	swap-out injection~\cite{Swap-out}, and longitudinal injection~\cite{PhysRevSTAB.18.020701}.
L000132	These developments have largely been motivated by advanced light-source facilities
L000133	where ultralow emittance of storage beam requires extremely precise control
L000134	and injection into very narrow dynamic apertures~\cite{Aiba_Review}.
L000135	
L000136	The present study addresses a different direction of progress.
L000137	We focus on the ultra-compact storage rings, since a smaller ring reduces the region
L000138	in which the experimental environment must be controlled for physics measurements,
L000139	for example with respect to magnetic field uniformity and the installation of large-scale detector components.
L000140	These features are especially important for next-generation precision-measurement experiments.
L000141	
L000142	\begin{figure*}[tbp]
L000143	    \centering
L000144	    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{SpiralInjection_v2.pdf}
L000145	    \caption{
L000146	        (a): Overview of the demonstration beamline.
L000147	        The electron beam is generated by an electron gun and injected into the storage magnet
L000148	        through a transport line consisting of three rotatable quadrupole magnets,
L000149	        one bending magnet,
L000150	        and a pair of steering magnets.
L000151	        (b) X-Z projection of the reference particle orbit after injection.
L000152	        The storage midplane corresponds to $Z = 0\,\si{cm}$.
L000153	        (c),(d) $B_r$ components along the reference particle orbit.
L000154	        Blue line shows the static magnetic field by the storage magnet.
L000155	        Red line shows the time-varying magnetic field by the kicker.
L000156	        The $B_r < 0$ field during injection provides the downward steering to electrons
L000157	        required for beam storage in weak-focusing region.
L000158	        }
L000159	    \label{fig:SITE_overview}
L000160	\end{figure*}
L000161	
L000162	However, ultra-compact storage rings face a fundamental difficulty.
L000163	As the size of the ring becomes smaller, the revolution period of the circulating beam decreases to a few nanoseconds.
L000164	Under these conditions, conventional injection schemes become challenging
L000165	because they require strong pulsed magnetic fields with nanosecond-scale rise and fall times.
L000166	Even state-of-the-art developments for the ILC damping ring demonstrated switching times of approximately $3\,\si{ns}$~\cite{ILC_Kicker}
L000167	, and achieving significantly faster performance remains technically demanding.
L000168	This limitation has formed a major obstacle in the realization of ultra-compact storage rings.
L000169	For nanosecond revolution period, injection with minimal perturbation requires a kick confined to single turn,
L000170	placing simultaneous demands on both switching speed and peak field that are difficult to meet with conventional pulsed-power systems.
L000171	
L000172	A concept proposed in 2016 by {\it H.~Iinuma et al.}~\cite{H.Iinuma2016} offers a solution.
L000173	The idea is known as the {\it three-dimensional spiral injection scheme},
L000174	and it avoids the time-scale limitation by extending the injection orbit into the vertical direction.
L000175	Instead of injecting the beam parallel to the solenoidal axis, the beam enters the solenoid-type storage magnet with a controlled pitch angle.
L000176	This non-parallel injection causes the beam to experience the fringe field of the solenoid, which provides an initial vertical steering force.
L000177	The storage region is defined by a weak-focusing potential~\cite{WF_RRWilson, WF_DWKerst} located near the mid-plane of the magnet.
L000178	As the injected beam enters the weak-focusing potential region, the radial field component $B_r$ changes sign due to the weak-focusing field, which reverses the vertical Lorentz force and steers the beam upward.
L000179	To counteract this effect, the spiral injection concept employs a pulsed kicker and this supplies a small vertical kick to reduces pitch angle during many consecutive turns.
L000180	
L000181	The accumulated effect of these repeated vertical kicks guides the injected beam into the weak-focusing potential,
L000182	allowing stable storage. Because the required deflection is distributed over multiple turns,
L000183	the method avoids the need for the extremely fast pulsed-power performance that limits conventional two-dimensional injection.
L000184	
L000185	The ability to implement this scheme paves the way toward ultra-compact storage rings that are impractical with conventional injection schemes.
L000186	The ultra-compact rings are essential for precision measurements involving short-lived particles.
L000187	The muon $g-2$/EDM experiment at J-PARC~\cite{E34} and the muEDM experiment at PSI~\cite{muEDM} require the storage of relativistic beams in regions only a few tens of centimeters across, with revolution periods of only a few nanoseconds.
L000188	Compact rings enable relativistic beams to be stored in a small, well-controlled volume,
L000189	which is advantageous for precision measurements of short-lived particles.
L000190	Beyond muon physics, ultra-compact weak-focusing rings could support high-precision mass spectrometry
L000191	and electric-dipole-moment searches using various particle species.
L000192	
L000193	No experimental demonstration had been reported so far.
L000194	In this Letter we present the first successful storage of an electron beam using this method.
L000195	
L000196	
L000197	
L000198	
L000199	
L000200	{\it Experimental setup}---
L000201	A beamline was constructed~\cite{RehmanThesis}
L000202	for the demonstration of the three-dimensional spiral injection scheme.
L000203	Fig.~\ref{fig:SITE_overview}(a) shows an overview of the demonstration beamline.
L000204	An electron beam with momentum is $p=297\,\si{keV/}c$, kinetic energy is $E_{\rm kin}=80\,\si{keV}$
L000205	and pulsed width is $100\,\si{ns}$ is generated
L000206	using a thermionic electron gun~\cite{E-gun} and a chopper system~\cite{R.Matsushita2021}.
L000207	The transport line allows us to control the beam phase space~\cite{H.Iinuma2026} and the injection orbit at the injection point.
L000208	This transport line consists of three quadrupole magnets, one bending magnet,
L000209	and a pair of steering magnets~\cite{RehmanThesis}
L000210	, then injected into the storage magnet with a $0.7\,\si{rad}$ pitch angle,
L000211	defined with respect to the horizontal (X-Y) plane.
L000212	
L000213	The storage magnet consists of two solenoidal coils~\cite{Rehman_LINAC18},
L000214	main coil and auxiliary coil shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:SITE_overview}(a),
L000215	allow us to apply both solenoidal field and weak-focusing field in the beam storage region.
L000216	By setting the coil currents $I_{\rm MAIN}$ and $I_{\rm AUX}$ with opposite polarities,
L000217	we adjust the weak-focusing field potential (field index $n\sim 10^{-2}$ in the storage region)
L000218	while keeping the solenoidal field constant at $B_z=8.77\,\si{mT}$ on the storage plane ($Z=0\,\si{cm}$).
L000219	Fig.~\ref{fig:SITE_overview}(b) shows the projected reference particle orbit in the X-Z plane
L000220	and Fig.~\ref{fig:SITE_overview}(c) and (d) show the corresponding $B_r$ component along the reference orbit.
L000221	After injection, the beam follows a spiral orbit thanks to the $B_z$ component and simultaneously
L000222	being steered downward ($Z < 0$) thanks to the fringe field of $B_r < 0$.
L000223	Inside the weak-focusing region, the $B_r > 0$ from static weak-focusing field applies an upward force.
L000224	To counter this, a $45\,\si{A}$, $140\,\si{ns}$ pulsed current is applied to the kicker coils,
L000225	inductance $L=1.3\,\si{\mu H}$, at $Z = \pm 15\,\si{cm}$,
L000226	generating a $B_r < 0$ field that maintains the downward steering and enables beam storage.
L000227	
L000228	A detector using plastic-scintillating-fiber (SciFi), {\it SciFi-probe}~\cite{R.Matsushita2024},
L000229	which can be inserted into the storage region, is utilized to measure the storage beams.
L000230	The SciFi-probe consists of a $1\,\si{mm}$-diameter and $20\,\si{cm}$-long SciFi,
L000231	which is long enough to cover the entire storage region vertically.
L000232	The scintillation signal is read out with a photomultiplier tube (PMT).
L000233	Because the CSDA range of a $p=297\,\si{keV/}c$ electron in the SciFi is about $100\,\si{\mu m}$
L000234	\footnote{The electron CSDA range is obtained from the NIST ESTAR database~\cite{NIST_STAR},
L000235	assuming polystyrene (PS) as a material for the scintillating fiber.}, the measurement is destructive.
L000236	
L000237	In a measurement, the SciFi-probe is inserted vertically from above
L000238	with its tip positioned at an insertion depth $Z$, which is measured from the storage midplane ($Z=0\,\si{cm}$),
L000239	and particle hits generate a signal.
L000240	Because stored particles perform vertical betatron oscillations,
L000241	the integrated signal at a given $Z$ is proportional to the population whose vertical amplitude exceeds that depth (Fig.~\ref{fig:SciFiprobe_Meas}).
L000242	Since the stored particles also perform betatron oscillations in the radial direction
L000243	simultaneously with vertical betatron oscillations,
L000244	the SciFi-probe does not measure all stored particles within a single vertical betatron oscillation period.
L000245	We thus integrate the SciFi-probe signal over a sufficiently long time window to cover a wide range of betatron phases.
L000246	In this Letter, we define beam storage operationally as observing a SciFi-probe signal
L000247	that exceeds $5\sigma_{\rm noise}$ for $1\,\si{\micro s}$ or longer,
L000248	which is ten times longer than the injected pulse width of $100\,\si{ns}$ and corresponds to more than $200$ revolutions,
L000249	where $\sigma_{\rm noise}$ is the standard deviation (rms fluctuation) of the voltage in a pre-injection time window.
L000250	This conservative criterion is introduced to distinguish true storage from non-stored or
L000251	transiently circulating particles that may survive for only a few turns
L000252	before escaping the weak-focusing region.
L000253	
L000254	\begin{figure}[t]
L000255	    \centering
L000256	    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{MeasSciFiProbe_VBOamp_ideal.pdf}
L000257	    \caption{
L000258	        Principle of SciFi-probe measurement.
L000259	        Solid lines show the stored particle trajectories with vertical betatron oscillation.
L000260	        Stored particles with vertical betatron amplitude greater than $Z\,\si{[cm]}$,
L000261	        which is the tip position of the SciFi-probe, generate signals.
L000262	        Case-1, SciFi-probe is inserted up to $Z = 3.5\,\si{cm}$, measures particles
L000263	        with vertical amplitude $\geqq 3.5\,\si{cm}$ shown by red lines.
L000264	        Similarly, Case-2, SciFi-probe is inserted up to $Z = 2.0\,\si{cm}$,
L000265	        measures those with amplitude $\geqq 2.0\,\si{cm}$ shown by red and blue lines.
L000266	    }
L000267	    \label{fig:SciFiprobe_Meas}
L000268	\end{figure}
L000269	
L000270	A plastic scintillator is installed on the bottom surface of the storage chamber
L000271	as a beam loss monitor to observe time structure of reflected beams
L000272	that are not captured in the storage region during injection.
L000273	Information from this beam loss monitor is used for tuning beam injection trajectory.
L000274	
L000275	\begin{figure}[thb]
L000276	    \centering
L000277	    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{MeasSignal_v2.pdf}
L000278	    \caption{
L000279	        Example of measured signals.
L000280	        (a): SciFi-probe signal measured within the weak-focusing region.
L000281	        Blue line shows the threshold of $5\sigma_{\rm noise}$.
L000282	        (b): Loss-monitor signal downstream of the storage region.
L000283	        (c): Kicker current waveform measured using a Rogowski coil.
L000284	        Red and black lines correspond to the with and without kicker conditions, respectively.
L000285	        In this example, the SciFi-probe is inserted up to the storage midplane
L000286	        and SciFi covered the range from $Z=0\,\si{cm}$ to $Z=20\,\si{cm}$.
L000287	        Each waveform is an average over $1000$ shots.
L000288	    }
L000289	    \label{fig:MeasSignal}
L000290	\end{figure}
L000291	
L000292	\begin{figure*}[tbp]
L000293	    \centering
L000294	    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{Dependence_WeakFocus_v2.pdf}
L000295	    \caption{
L000296	        Weak-focusing field dependence of the stored beam distribution.
L000297	        (a): Weak-focusing field configurations.
L000298	        Colored points denote measurement result, and colored lines denote
L000299	        finite element calculations performed with Opera~\cite{Opera}.
L000300	        (b): $Z$-scan results under the four field configurations.
L000301	        The vertical axis shows the time-integrated SciFi-probe signal,
L000302	        $I_{\rm Signal}=\int V_{\rm Signal}(t)\,dt$,
L000303	        where $V_{\rm Signal}(t)$ is the measured voltage as a function of time.
L000304	        The integral is evaluated over the time window from $t=560\,\si{ns}$ to $9000\,\si{ns}$,
L000305	        starting just after the end of the kicker pulse.
L000306	        (c): Comparison of measured stored beam ranges with Monte Carlo predictions.
L000307	        Blue shaded regions show the expected region of MC simulation.
L000308	        Black points show the measurement result from field measurement and Z-scan measurement.
L000309	        Here the edge point is defined as the $Z$ position where $I_{\rm Signal}$ decreases to $5\%$ of its maximum value.
L000310	        For the measured points, the vertical uncertainty is dominated by the SciFi-probe positioning uncertainty and shot-to-shot fluctuations,
L000311	        while the horizontal uncertainty is dominated by the magnetic-field measurement accuracy.
L000312	    }
L000313	    \label{fig:WeakFocusDependency}
L000314	\end{figure*}
L000315	
L000316	
L000317	
L000318	
L000319	
L000320	{\it Experimental results}---
L000321	    Beam storage was confirmed using the operational criterion defined above based on the SciFi-probe waveform.
L000322	Fig.~\ref{fig:MeasSignal} shows the waveforms from the SciFi-probe, the beam-loss monitor and kicker current for cases with and without the kicker.
L000323	With the kicker activated, the SciFi-probe signal remains above $5\sigma_{\rm noise}$ for longer than $1\,\si{\micro s}$,
L000324	thereby satisfying our definition of beam storage and indicating successful beam storage in the weak-focusing region.
L000325	The beam-loss monitor simultaneously detected a signal induced by reflected beams, at the expected timing relative to the kicker pulse.
L000326	In contrast, without the kicker the SciFi-probe signal has a duration of order $100\,\si{ns}$ comparable to the injected pulse width
L000327	and does not satisfy the $5\sigma_{\rm noise}$ for $1\,\si{\micro s}$ storage criterion,
L000328	indicating that the beam is not stored under these conditions.
L000329	This clear contrast demonstrates that three-dimensional spiral injection enables beam storage in ultra-compact storage rings.
L000330	
L000331	During the first several hundred nanoseconds after injection, the stored particles perform coherent vertical betatron oscillations.
L000332	This coherence produced a periodic modulation in the SciFi waveform. Although the modulation originates from the vertical betatron motion,
L000333	its period does not correspond to the betatron oscillation period itself.
L000334	The difference arises because the injected beam has a pulse width that is longer than one betatron period,
L000335	so the SciFi-probe samples particles with a wide distribution of betatron phases within each injection pulse.
L000336	As time evolves, the periodic structure gradually decreases in visibility.
L000337	This reduction is caused by the position dependence of the weak-focusing magnetic field,
L000338	which introduces small variations in the betatron frequency and leads to phase mixing among the stored particles.
L000339	
L000340	The measured storage signal persisted for $\geq 1\,\si{\micro\second}$, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:MeasSignal}(a).
L000341	This duration is more than one order of magnitude longer than the loss time observed without the kicker and demonstrates
L000342	that multi-turn vertical steering enables stable beam storage even when the revolution period is as short as $4.7\,\si{ns}$.
L000343	The observed signal duration is largely limited by scattering in the SciFi-probe, which is inserted into the storage region for measurement.
L000344	It therefore provides a lower bound on the intrinsic storage lifetime of the beam, which is expected to be longer than the observed value.
L000345	
L000346	We verified that the accumulated beam is stored in the weak-focusing field by measuring its vertical distribution
L000347	under four different field configurations.
L000348	The corresponding magnetic-field distributions are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:WeakFocusDependency}(a).
L000349	For each configuration, we performed a scan of the SciFi-probe insertion depth $Z$, which is measured from the storage midplane,
L000350	hereafter referred to as a {\it $Z$-scan}:
L000351	the SciFi-probe was inserted from above in steps of $5\,\si{mm}$, and at each $Z$ we measured a waveform averaged over $1000 \,\si{shots}$.
L000352	We then evaluated the time-integrated value $I_{\rm Signal}$, the definition given in the caption of Fig.~\ref{fig:WeakFocusDependency},
L000353	which yields the $Z$-scan curve shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:WeakFocusDependency}(b).
L000354	In Fig.~\ref{fig:WeakFocusDependency}(c), we define the upper edge of the stored-beam distribution as the $Z$ position
L000355	where $I_{\rm Signal}$ decreases to $5\%$ of its maximum value,
L000356	and compare it with Monte Carlo (MC) predictions of the storable range for each configuration.
L000357	The vertical uncertainty of the measured points includes
L000358	(i) the positioning uncertainty of the SciFi-probe
L000359	and (ii) shot-to-shot fluctuations of the $I_{\rm Signal}$,
L000360	whereas the horizontal uncertainty is dominated by the measurement accuracy of the weak-focusing field distribution
L000361	used to determine the storable range for each configuration.
L000362	In the MC predictions, the shaded region represents the spread obtained by including the injection-trajectory uncertainty,
L000363	which is the dominant systematic contribution.
L000364	The measurements for all configurations agree with the MC predictions,
L000365	demonstrating that the observed stored-beam distribution is governed by the intended weak-focusing field configuration
L000366	rather than accidental trapping or experimental artifacts.
L000367	
L000368	The present storage efficiency, defined as the fraction of electrons stored from one injected bunch,
L000369	is well below $1\%$ under the current injection conditions based on Monte Carlo simulations.
L000370	The storage efficiency can be improved by XY-coupled transverse phase-space matching~\cite{H.Iinuma_IPAC25, S.Ogawa_IPAC25}
L000371	and a shorter injected bunch length achievable through upstream RF beam manipulation.

L000377	{\it Conclusions}---
L000378	We have achieved the first experimental demonstration of beam storage by the three-dimensional spiral injection scheme.
L000379	This demonstration establishes the technical feasibility of this scheme
L000380	and provides a viable pathway toward ultra-compact storage rings
L000381	required for next-generation precision experiments.
L000382	The technique is a key enabling technique for the planned muon $g-2$/EDM experiment at J-PARC
L000383	and the muEDM experiment at PSI,
L000384	and may open a new frontier in precision studies of short-lived particles.
